reason: The hub is a name-to-backend table plus a map of mounted data forms and does no I/O itself. With one database and no interchangeable backends there is nothing left for it to register, so it is not built.

The typed API that product code uses (declared domains, validated records, one write queue, a change event) is kept in substance as the kv package: namespaces in one table, a version per record, one transaction per update, and a change notice that also covers writes by other processes.
The JSON file backend rewrites a whole unit per write, has no cross-process lock and no crash-atomic batch. Machine state moves to tables in the one database, so no JSON state backend is built.

Its document-per-row idea survives as the kv table, but inside the one harness database opened by the session store's driver package, not as a second database with its own open sequence and layout version.

The attachment seam is kept as a Go contract package: opaque identifiers, references in events, all-or-none batch admission, stable error codes and verify-on-read. It gains size limits for generic files, a Touch step before an event cites a stored reference, and streaming reads.

The local provider keeps content-addressed files under the harness home, staged, synced and published by exclusive link, with the image pipeline rewritten on pure-Go decoders. The content-address mechanics become a blob service other areas also use, and it gains reference rows, garbage collection and a per-process decoded-pixel budget.

The spill storage seam is kept as a Go contract package. The one-method interface grows to reserve, create (a writer for text or a stream), open, stat and delete, so that retention and access by session lineage are part of the contract.

Private files with random names and exclusive owner-only creation are kept. Files always live under the harness home instead of a per-process temporary directory, and the start-up sweep becomes part of the timed maintenance duty.

The policy that replaces an oversized tool result with a head and tail preview and a notice is kept as a listener on the pipeline's shape-and-bound stage. Its budget has no off value, it bounds the result even when saving fails, and it marks the result with a structured field.

The workspace registry is kept: canonical-path records, a session ledger, order, pin and archive with the rule that archive never hides running work. It moves to real tables with one transaction per mutation, and activity providers become a Go interface.

The settings service is kept as forms over the live fields of composed entries, validated against the whole config and written only through config.Service.Apply of the boot area, which owns the one writable layer. The legacy settings.yaml import is not carried because no Go release wrote that file.
Every citing event gets a reference row in its append transaction and a draft lists its references, and a maintenance duty deletes objects that neither names once they are older than a grace period.

The two cases where a machine-local store hurts are covered: a remote execution world reads an attachment by identifier through the host, and a session export carries its objects by digest. Two machines sharing one live store is excluded because the home must be on a local filesystem.

The model still receives the first frame, but an animated source now keeps its original bytes as a linked file object, so the transcript can show the animation and nothing the user attached is discarded.

Output bytes no longer depend on an installed native library build: the encoders are Go code pinned by go.mod and the toolchain, and a transform version is part of every cache identity so an upgrade re-addresses variants without invalidating stored objects.

Generic files get a per-file size limit and a per-message count limit enforced while streaming, which removes the unbounded case. Audio and video remain generic files by decision and are listed as a limitation.
Attachments are collected by a reference-aware maintenance duty: an object no session event or draft cites is deleted after the grace period.

A draft record per session in the machine-state store holds the unsent text and lists its staged uploads, which the collector treats as references, so a draft and its files survive a reload or restart; the composer area writes the record.

A form addresses an entry by its id in the composed tree, and the one writable layer may hold a merge operation for any entry, whichever file or bundle supplied it; there are no separately owned include documents.
The form has two distinct operations: reset removes the user's override so the lower value is inherited, and clear writes the merge operation's null, which deletes a value a lower layer supplies.
The sweep is part of a maintenance duty that runs at start and on a timer in whichever process holds the duty lease, so a long-running host is swept without a restart.

The locator is the host path mapped through the filesystem seam, and where the active provider cannot map it the spill_read tool reads the file on the host, so retrieval does not need a co-located filesystem consumer.
The logged tool result carries a structured spill field that only the policy sets; the user interface and retention read that field and never recognise a notice by its text.
A missing image calculator falls back to a fixed image cost and an unreadable image path omits the image with a statement, so the result is bounded in every case instead of staying inline in full.

The store reserves a fixed-size id before writing, the notice is sized first, and configuration rejects a budget smaller than the largest possible notice, so a notice always fits and no file is saved and then left unreferenced.
The Go contract includes Open, Stat and Delete beside Save, so retrieval, lifetime and deletion are defined at the seam and not left to each backend.

The store's own retrieval method checks that the calling session owns the file or was forked from the owner. Reading the path with a file tool remains possible for any session of the same user, which is the general unconfined-read gap stated in design.md section 6 and not a property of this seam.

Every write increases a stored namespace revision in its transaction; another process compares the revision before a gating read and on a timer, reloads, and raises the change notice with origin foreign.
An update is one SQL transaction that may touch any number of records, and state that needs indexes, uniqueness or composite keys (the workspace ledger) is stored in real tables.
Each record stores the version of the type it was written with and a registered converter upgrades it when read; a change no converter can express uses the database's forward-only layout migration.
There is no whole-file JSON unit: a write changes the rows it touches in one transaction.
Writers in different processes are serialised by the database with a bounded wait and one classified busy error, so no write is lost to a later file replacement.
No machine-state file is published by rename any more. The files this area still writes (blobs and the request cache) go through the one fsx helper, which states its durability on each platform.
A batch delete is one database transaction, so a crash leaves all of it or none of it and no staging residue.
The limit exists because Node runs JavaScript on one thread and its built-in SQLite driver is synchronous; in Go a database call blocks one goroutine and the rest of the process keeps running.
Every connection to the one database uses the same bounded busy wait and returns one classified busy error when it expires, which the kv layer passes on as storage/busy.
The tables of this area are part of the one database's layout, which is migrated forward in one transaction after an automatic backup instead of being rejected.
The version is a column of every record, so a record written by an older or newer build is recognised on its own and one bad record does not decide the fate of the whole unit.
There is one database file opened by one driver package; this area has no open sequence of its own to duplicate.
There are no backend facets. The session log has its own store in the same database, and machine state uses typed tables, so a deferred log facet has nothing to wait for.
A consumer injects the store by a typed service key and is not constructed until the service is provided, so a too-early read that throws cannot happen and entry order does not matter.

Session deletion now exists in the session store, and removing a workspace can cascade to it on request. The folder is never deleted by the harness, which is a recorded decision and not a missing capability.

Membership is validated once, when the session is attached and its directory resolves to the workspace, and stored as a row. Nothing is re-derived from a path later, so a missing path raises no question the store cannot answer.
Directory status is read from the filesystem when the list is rendered, with a two-second cache, so a change made outside the harness shows without a refresh or restart.
Archive and pin flags are rows that reference the sessions table and are deleted with the session, so a flag for a missing session cannot exist and both directions apply the same existence rule.

Archiving writes a pending mark first, which the step gate already treats as blocked, then asks the activity providers, then confirms or removes the mark. A turn that starts after the mark is blocked and one that started before it is reported.
Adding a workspace can adopt the ungrouped sessions whose recorded directory resolves to it, so re-adding a removed directory brings its sessions back when the user asks for that.
The Go Add operation takes no title parameter; the title defaults to the directory name and Rename changes it, so the unused parameter does not exist.

title: A settings edit stores the entry's complete config in the profile row, so later bundle changes to its other fields never reach that profile

reason: A settings edit writes a merge operation that holds only the edited fields, so every other field of the entry keeps following the lower layers.

title: With no configured root, spill files land in a per-process directory under the system temporary directory, so a resumed session's locators point into an old directory

reason: Spill files always live under the harness home in a directory derived from the session, so a locator written by an earlier process still resolves after a restart.

Replaced by the typed notify event kv.Changed, raised after commit in commit order per namespace with namespace, key, operation, revision and origin; it also reports writes made by another process, which upstream's in-process event cannot.
Replaced by the typed notify event settings.FormChanged with the entry id and the entry revision of the boot area, raised when the loader announces a settled reload and a form's revision differs.

The waterfall becomes the Report method of a registered workspace.ActivityProvider interface whose results are concatenated, so one provider cannot drop another's answer and a failing provider counts as activity.
The parallel event becomes the Stop method of the same ActivityProvider interface, called for every provider at once after the archive is durable, with failures aggregated and logged.
Kept as the typed event workspace.SessionArchived in the parallel dispatch form: listeners register follow-up work and return, and a failure is logged without undoing the archive.
Kept as the typed event workspace.SessionUnarchiving in the parallel dispatch form: any listener failure keeps the session archived.

Replaced by the Go struct attachments.Config with the same nine image limits and defaults; the home override is gone, the concurrency count becomes a decoded-pixel budget, and limits for generic files and the request cache are added.
Replaced by the Go struct spill.StoreConfig with a maximum age (30 days by default) and a maximum save size; the root option is gone because files always live under the harness home.
Replaced by the Go struct spill.PolicyConfig: the token budget has a default and a validated minimum and no off value, and a fallback image cost is added.
The config chooses a default backend and per-domain routes. With one database there is no backend to choose, so the config has no subject.
The config names the root directory of the JSON backend, which is not built.

The config names a database path and a journal mode. The Go design has one database at a fixed place in the harness home, and WAL is required because several processes share it, so neither field remains.
ctx.attachments becomes the service key attachments.Key with the interface attachments.Store, a direct seam whose provider is the local store component.

ctx.settings becomes the service key settings.Key with the interface settings.Forms, provided by a component that reads the composed tree from config.Service of the boot area and writes only through config.Service.Apply.
ctx.spillStore becomes the service key spill.Key with the interface spill.Store, a direct seam whose provider is the local spill component.
ctx.storage is the hub's registration table for backends and data forms; no hub exists in the Go design, so no service replaces it.
ctx.storageDomain becomes the service key kv.Key with the interface kv.Store, which opens typed namespaces in the one database instead of domains over routed backends.
ctx.workspaceRegistry becomes the service key workspace.Key with the interface workspace.Registry, which also holds the registry of activity providers.

The three roles (storage interface, local backend, policy) and the bounded preview with a locator the model reads later are kept. Three things change: a failed save still bounds the result, the reference is a structured field and not recognised text, and the store gains read, delete and reference-aware retention.

The need the note states (a home for data that belongs to no single session, and a workspace entity that owns a session list) is kept. The hub with pluggable backends and routes is not: the first verdict called a backend registry a good fit, but DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-9 drops the hub, and machine state is typed tables in the one database.

Both ideas are kept by different means. Everything is under the harness home, resolved once at start. Authority is declared per namespace: an undecodable record is dropped from a derived namespace and fails the owner of an authoritative one; damage to the medium itself is damage to the one database, which the session store area handles.

Kept: every value is declared once in its component's config type, settings only lists live fields and writes to the one writable layer, and an edit a higher layer would shadow fails before saving. The loader's merge operation removes the note's side effect that an edit pins the entry's other fields, and the legacy settings.yaml import has nothing to import.

Kept: archive refuses while work runs, stops it on request after the durable write, and no model step runs for an archived session. Providers become a Go interface, a pending mark closes the window between the check and the write, and the flags are rows so that the rule holds when another process holds the session.

Adopted although upstream has not built it: an unreadable image is recorded by a logged quarantine event and replaced with deterministic text by a message projection, so one lost file does not end a session and every request stays reconstructable from the log.

Workspace identity by canonical path, attach validation, one workspace per session, cascade on session delete, adopt on add
